section.title: The Two Baskets of Figs
section.sectionRationale: A short, sharp vision reverses everyone's expectations: the exiles already carried off to Babylon, the ones who looked like the losers, are the good figs God regards for good, while those who remained in Jerusalem and Zedekiah's court, who seemed to have escaped judgment, are the bad figs marked for disaster.
section.thesis: God's favor does not follow appearances or circumstances; the exiles who seem cast off are the good figs He will watch over for good and give a new heart to know Him, while those who seem to have kept their place are the bad figs already appointed to ruin.
section.frameNote: Three scenes: the vision of two baskets set before the temple, the good figs identified as the exiles marked for restoration, and the bad figs identified as Zedekiah and the remnant marked for disaster.

units.label: The vision of two baskets
units.note: very good figs and very bad figs

verses.text: After Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried away Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim king of Judah, as well as the officials of Judah and the craftsmen and metalsmiths from Jerusalem, and had brought them to Babylon, the LORD showed me two baskets of figs placed in front of the temple of the LORD.
One basket had very good figs, like those that ripen early, but the other basket contained very poor figs, so bad they could not be eaten.

“Jeremiah,” the LORD asked, “what do you see?” 
“Figs!” I replied. “The good figs are very good, but the bad figs are very bad, so bad they cannot be eaten.”

units.label: The good figs, a heart to know Me

verses.text: Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Like these good figs, so I regard as good the exiles from Judah, whom I have sent away from this place to the land of the Chaldeans.
I will keep My eyes on them for good and will return them to this land. I will build them up and not tear them down; I will plant them and not uproot them.
I will give them a {{lev|heart}} to {{yada|know}} Me, that I am the LORD. They will be My people, and I will be their God, for they will return to Me with all their heart.

units.label: The bad figs, appointed for disaster
units.note: Zedekiah and the remnant left behind

verses.text: But like the bad figs, so bad they cannot be eaten,’ says the LORD, ‘so will I deal with Zedekiah king of Judah, his officials, and the remnant of Jerusalem, those remaining in this land and those living in the land of Egypt.
I will make them a horror and an offense to all the kingdoms of the earth, a disgrace and an object of scorn, ridicule, and cursing wherever I have banished them.
And I will send against them sword and famine and plague, until they have perished from the land that I gave to them and their fathers.’”

lev.gloss: Heart, the seat of thought, will, and desire in Hebrew, not merely emotion. God promises to give the exiles a new lev to know Him, an inward transformation rather than only an outward change of circumstance, a promise that grows into the full new covenant language of Jeremiah 31:33.

yada.gloss: To know, in Hebrew a rich word for intimate, relational knowledge, not merely factual information. God's promise that the exiles will have a heart to yada Him describes covenant relationship restored from the inside, exactly what verse 16 of chapter 22 also calls knowing the LORD.

basic.context: After Babylon's first deportation of Judah's leaders and skilled workers, God shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs at the temple, one full of excellent figs, one full of figs so rotten they cannot be eaten. The shock of the vision is who is who: the exiles already carried off to Babylon, who looked like the ones who had lost everything, are the good figs God will watch over for good, while King Zedekiah and those who remained in the land, who seemed to have escaped judgment, are the bad figs marked for disaster.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a straightforward symbolic vision with its meaning explained directly in the text itself, no guesswork required, God states plainly which basket represents which group and why. The challenge for readers is resisting the natural assumption that whoever suffers most visibly must be under God's greatest judgment; this vision insists the opposite is often true, present suffering can be the very context of God's deepest future mercy.
basic.originalLanguages: The heart of the promise to the exiles is that God will give them a new lev, heart, to yada, know, Him, language of inward transformation and intimate relationship rather than mere external return to the land. This same pairing of heart and knowing God anticipates the fuller new covenant promise later in Jeremiah 31:33-34, where God writes His law on the heart itself.
basic.typology: The exile that looked like pure catastrophe becomes, in this vision, the very context of God's saving purpose, a pattern that anticipates how God works redemption through apparent defeat, most fully through the cross, where what looked like total loss became the means of salvation. The promise of a new heart to know God anticipates the new covenant of chapter 31 and its fulfillment in the Spirit's inward work through Christ.
basic.christ: The promise of a heart to know God, given specifically to a people in exile and disgrace, anticipates the new covenant Christ inaugurates, where God's Spirit writes His law within and gives believers the very knowledge of God this vision promises, Hebrews 8:10-11. Just as the exiles' apparent loss became the setting for God's deepest work of grace, Christ's own apparent defeat on the cross becomes the very means of the world's redemption.
basic.god: God's favor does not track with visible circumstances; He sees and values what human observers would overlook or dismiss, choosing the exiles, not those who remained comfortably in Jerusalem, as the objects of His restoring grace. Yet God is equally just, refusing to soften His verdict on Zedekiah and those who trusted their apparent safety instead of turning to Him.
basic.crossReferences: Jeremiah 31:33 develops this same heart-transformation promise into the full new covenant. Hebrews 8:10-11 quotes that new covenant directly, showing its fulfillment in Christ. 1 Corinthians 1:27-29 shows God consistently choosing the lowly and despised to shame what seems strong. Romans 8:28 echoes the pattern that God works even hard circumstances for the good of those who love Him.
basic.oneStory: The two baskets of figs show that God's redemptive purposes often run precisely opposite to human appearances, choosing the exiled and apparently rejected as the ones He is quietly preparing for restoration and a new heart. That pattern reaches its fullest expression in Christ, whose apparent defeat on the cross became the very means by which God gives His people new hearts to truly know Him.

context.literary:
The chapter is a compact vision report with the same three-part rhythm Jeremiah uses elsewhere: the LORD shows, the LORD asks, "what do you see?", and the LORD interprets. The pattern already appeared in the call, where Jeremiah saw an almond branch and a boiling pot, 1:11-13, and the form here is the same. A vision whose meaning is handed over at once leaves the reader no time to guess; what is startling is not the code but the verdict.

The report is symmetrical. Verses 1 to 3 describe the two baskets, 4 to 7 give the good figs a fourfold promise, and 8 to 10 give the bad figs a fourfold sentence. The promise and the sentence mirror each other. The good figs are watched 'for good', built and not torn down, planted and not uprooted, and given a heart; the bad figs are made a horror, a disgrace, a curse and a byword, and visited with sword, famine and plague. The two halves cannot be understood separately, and the chapter's force is in the way they are set side by side.

A reversal inside the language deserves notice. Jeremiah was called 'to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant', 1:10. In 24:6 the verbs come back, but now only in their kind half: build, plant, not tear down, not uproot. The vision shows the call of the book being applied, with the destructive verbs aimed at one basket and the constructive ones at the other.

The date is carefully placed in verse 1: after the deportation of Jeconiah, but before the final fall. The chapter therefore sits between chapters 21 to 23, with their judgments on the kings, and the letter to the exiles in chapter 29, which carries the same verdict on the same two groups, 29:16-19. It also stands at the end of a section that has asked who will lead God's people, and tells us that the leadership of the future is in Babylon.
context.historical:
The vision is dated to the months after the first great deportation. In 597 BC Nebuchadnezzar took King Jeconiah, the queen mother, the officials, the soldiers and the craftsmen to Babylon, 2 Kings 24:12-16, and the text says only the poorest people of the land remained, 24:14. Daniel had been taken a few years earlier, Daniel 1:1-6, and Ezekiel was among this group, which explains why the exiles of this deportation were the men who would later write and shape Israel's faith in captivity. Nebuchadnezzar installed Zedekiah, Jeconiah's uncle, on the throne, 2 Kings 24:17.

The people left in Jerusalem drew the obvious conclusion. They were still in the land, the temple still stood, and a king of David's line still reigned. The exiles, in their view, had been judged and the city spared. Ezekiel records the reasoning in his own words: the people of Jerusalem said of the exiles, 'They are far away from the LORD; this land has been given to us as a possession', Ezekiel 11:15. The vision of the figs is the LORD's answer to the same boast, given to a prophet in the city.

The baskets were placed 'in front of the temple', and the choice of setting is pointed. Baskets of first fruits were brought to the sanctuary at harvest, Deuteronomy 26:2, and the fig, like the vine, was one of Israel's emblems, Hosea 9:10. The early fig, ripe in early summer before the main crop, was a delicacy people ate eagerly, as Isaiah 28:4 shows. A basket of such figs by the temple looked like a gift. The other basket was fruit that could not be eaten. The difference could not have been seen from outside the vision.

The 'remnant of Jerusalem' includes those in Egypt, 24:8. Refugees had been going there since the reign of Jehoiakim, and the later flight after Gedaliah's murder lies ahead, so the verse sweeps up everyone who clung to the land or fled the crisis instead of turning to God.
context.canonical:
The figs belong to a family of agricultural images that run through the prophets. In Hosea 9:10 God says He found Israel like the first fruit of the fig tree in its first season, and in Jeremiah 8:13 the fig tree has no figs. Amos has a basket of summer fruit, 8:1-2, whose point is that the end has come, and Micah 7:1 mourns that there is no early fig to satisfy him. Jeremiah's baskets are the most developed use of the image, because they sort one people into two.

The same pair of verdicts appears in Jeremiah's letter to the exiles. In chapter 29 the people in Babylon are told to build houses, plant gardens and seek the welfare of the city, 29:5-7, while those left in Jerusalem are the 'rotten figs, so bad they cannot be eaten', 29:17. The vision gives the picture, and the letter turns it into instruction.

The promise of a heart to know God is the first sketch of what Jeremiah develops in chapters 31 and 32. The new covenant of 31:31-34 puts the law within, and 32:39 gives 'one heart and one way'. Ezekiel carries the same hope forward with the promise of a new heart and a new spirit, Ezekiel 36:26, and Deuteronomy 29:4 had earlier said that to that day the LORD had not given Israel a mind to understand. The vision looks back to Moses' sorrow and forward to the new covenant.

In the New Testament the language of the new covenant is quoted in full in Hebrews 8:8-12. And the exile's theme, a people sent out of the place of belonging yet loved by God, becomes a name for the church: Peter writes to 'the elect who are exiles', 1 Peter 1:1, and the writer to the Hebrews calls believers to go to Christ outside the camp, Hebrews 13:13. Jesus himself uses a fig tree to say that fruit is what counts, Luke 13:6-9.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Jeremiah wanted two audiences to hear this vision. To the exiles, it was the first word of real hope. They had been uprooted, humiliated and told by prophets that they were forgotten. Jeremiah gave them a different account: God had sent them away, 24:5, which means the deportation was His act and not an accident of the empire's strength, and He had His eyes on them for good. The exile was not the end of the story.

To those who remained, the vision was a warning meant to break complacency. They had made their survival a proof of favour, and Jeremiah's task was to tell them that survival is not the test. The 'bad figs' do not become bad when God judges them; they are bad when He shows them, because their rot is already in them.

The vision also teaches how to read circumstances. What looks like blessing may be ripening for judgment, and what looks like curse may be the place where God does His deepest work. Jeremiah was formed by exactly that experience, and the hearers were meant to learn it too.

The promise of verse 7 is the heart of the passage. God will not only bring the exiles home; He will give them a heart to know Him. The first hearers were meant to understand that the real problem of Judah was never its geography but its heart, and that restoration would begin there.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records a vision and God's explanation of it for a specific historical moment. The identification of who is a good fig and who is a bad one is a verdict about the exiles of 597 and the people of Zedekiah's day. It is not a rule that those who suffer deportation are always favoured or that those who stay are always rejected.

Nor does the passage claim that every individual exile was righteous. The 'good figs' are a company that God regards as good in His purposes, and what makes them good is the work He promises to do in them, 'I will give them a heart to know Me', not a prior record. The goodness is gift, not achievement. In the same way the passage should not be read as promising that every kind of hardship becomes a blessing, only that God was at work in this exile and promises to be in His people's trials.

What carries over is the warning against confusing comfort with favour and the invitation to trust that God is working where we cannot see. The vision also gives a template for how to look at suffering that has been caused by sin: it may be real discipline, and still be the way God brings His people to a new heart. Believers can take this as an assurance without making it a formula.

debates.question: Why would God favor the exiles, who suffered the trauma of deportation, over those who remained safely in the land?

views.label: Exile as disciplined grace, not mere punishment
views.case: The exiles' removal, though painful, put them in the place where God would work a new heart in them, verse 7, showing that hardship under God's hand can be the very context of His deepest transforming grace.

views.label: Remaining in Jerusalem as false security
views.case: Those who remained, especially under Zedekiah, presumed on their continued presence in the land as proof of God's favor, when in fact their persistence in the same sins that caused the first deportation only stored up greater judgment.

debates.bearing: Both observations converge on the same lesson: outward circumstances, whether suffering or apparent safety, are not reliable indicators of God's favor; only genuine turning to Him is.

debates.question: Is the verdict on the figs corporate or individual?

views.label: A corporate verdict on two communities
views.case: The baskets stand for groups: the exiles on one side, and Zedekiah, his officials and the remnant in Jerusalem and Egypt on the other, 24:5 and 24:8. God's dealing is with a people, and the promise that 'they will be My people' is a covenant promise made to a community.

views.label: Individual responsibility is still in play
views.case: Jeremiah elsewhere says that each will die for his own iniquity, 31:30, and Ezekiel 18:20 insists that a son does not bear his father's guilt. On this view a member of either group could still turn or harden, and the baskets describe the general direction of each company, not the fate of every person.

debates.bearing: The vision speaks of the group, and the promise of a heart to know God is the means by which individuals come to share in it. Neither reading permits a person to assume his place in the right basket by location alone; each hearer is still called to return to the LORD with all his heart, verse 7.

study.originalLanguages:
The vision begins with a pair of words the Bible's first chapters have taught us to hear. The good figs are tov, 'very good', and the bad are ra, 'very bad', in 24:2 and 24:3, the same two words that make up 'good and evil' in Genesis 2:17 and 3:5. A vision in which fruit is sorted into good and evil, set before the house of the LORD, quietly recalls the garden where humans first tried to take that judgment for themselves. Here God keeps it in His own hands and makes the sorting.

Look at the verb of verse 6, 'I will keep My eyes on them for good'. To set one's eyes on someone is to attend to them with care, and the phrase 'for good' reverses a pattern in the book. In 21:10 God says, 'I have set My face against this city to bring disaster and not good'. The same grammar, God's face or eyes set toward something, can mean judgment or blessing, and the exiles receive the second.

The four verbs, build, not tear down, plant, not uproot, are the verbs of Jeremiah's own commission, 1:10, and in 24:6 they come in their gentle form. Elsewhere in the book the same four are the programme of 18:7-9 and 31:28. The vision's promise is that the prophet's work, which has been mostly demolition, will in the end turn toward construction.

The heart of the promise is 'a heart to know Me'. The noun lev, heart, in Hebrew is the seat of mind and will as much as of feeling. To give a heart to know is to give the capacity to understand and to respond. The verb 'give', natan, appears for a gift God makes that people cannot make for themselves, and Deuteronomy 29:4 had said that God had not yet given Israel a mind to understand. The sentence in verse 7 is the answer to Moses' complaint. And 'know', yada, is the verb of relationship, the same one used of a man knowing his wife, so the exiles are promised not a doctrine but a bond.

The covenant formula, 'They will be My people, and I will be their God', is a standard expression of the relationship, and here it is the result of the new heart and not its precondition. The grammar of the verse makes the return to God a consequence: 'for they will return to Me with all their heart'. The verb 'return', shuv, is the book's great verb of repentance, and in this verse God both gives the heart and receives the return.

The bad figs are given a string of shaming words in verse 9. The 'horror' is the same word used of the people in 15:4, and the whole string of shame, scorn and cursing recalls the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28:37. The language is the standard language of the curses, so the fate of the bad figs is the fulfilment of the covenant sanctions that the people had agreed to.

typology.type: The exile as the place where God plants
typology.fulfillment: The exiles are sent away yet planted and built up, 24:6. A pattern runs through the Bible of life coming from a place of apparent loss: Joseph in Egypt, Genesis 50:20, Israel in the wilderness, and the seed that falls into the ground, John 12:24. In Christ the pattern is complete. His death, which looked like abandonment by God, is the planting from which a harvest comes, 1 Corinthians 15:20-23. The type falls short because the exiles were disciplined for their own sin, while Christ went into the ground for the sin of others.

typology.type: The heart given to know God
typology.fulfillment: The promise of a heart to know the LORD is the first sketch of the new covenant. Jeremiah 31:33 puts the law within, Ezekiel 36:26 gives a heart of flesh, and Hebrews 8:10 shows these promises fulfilled in Christ's work. The correspondence is that God Himself does what the people could not do. The escalation is that the new covenant is sealed in the blood of Christ and the Spirit is poured out on all who believe, Luke 22:20 and Acts 2:17. The exiles who received the first fruits of this promise did not see the whole of it, and the type is still unfolding.

typology.type: The baskets at the temple and the sorting of a people
typology.fulfillment: Two baskets are set before the temple and the people are divided between them, not by appearance but by what God has determined. The sorting at the temple anticipates the way Jesus' coming divides people: the ones who seem to have a place, like the Pharisees who trusted in their standing, are exposed, and tax collectors and prostitutes enter the kingdom first, Matthew 21:31. Jesus told a parable of a fig tree that bore no fruit, Luke 13:6-9, with the same logic that a position near God's house is no guarantee. The correspondence is in the principle, not in a fulfilment of the vision itself.

typology.type: The exile of God's people as a pilgrimage
typology.fulfillment: The exiles in Babylon are a people sent to a foreign land, charged to live well there, Jeremiah 29:5-7, until God brings them home. The New Testament applies the pattern to the church: believers are 'exiles' scattered through the world, 1 Peter 1:1, who seek a better country, Hebrews 11:13-16, and are called to bear the disgrace of Christ outside the camp, Hebrews 13:13. The pattern is partial, since the church's home is not a place on earth but the city that is to come, and the return is not from Babylon but from death.

study.christ:
The vision points to Christ along three lines. The first is the new heart. The God who promises 'a heart to know Me' is the God who, in the new covenant, writes His law within His people, and Hebrews 8:10-12 quotes the great promise of Jeremiah 31 as fulfilled in Jesus. The knowledge of God that the exiles are promised is not a matter of information. John says that eternal life is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom He sent, John 17:3. The giving of a heart to know is the work of the Spirit, which Jesus promised would come to those who are His, John 14:16-17.

The second is the pattern of loss that becomes the ground of life. The good figs are the people who appear to have lost everything, and God sees them as His. That is Christ's own path. Isaiah wrote of One who was despised and rejected by men, Isaiah 53:3, and Paul says that God chose what is low and despised so that no one may boast, 1 Corinthians 1:27-29. Jesus was carried out of the city to die, Hebrews 13:12, and the place of His shame is the place where the new covenant is sealed. He is the first fruits from the dead, 1 Corinthians 15:20, and He reverses the logic by which Jerusalem judged the exiles. Those who share in His reproach share in His life.

The third is the sorting of the people. The prophet's vision says that being near the temple is not enough. Jesus did the same when He said that tax collectors and prostitutes were entering the kingdom ahead of the chief priests and elders, Matthew 21:31, and when He lamented over Jerusalem, Luke 13:34-35. The temple setting of the baskets looks forward to the One who is greater than the temple, Matthew 12:6, and before whom all are shown for what they are.

The vision also gives the pastoral shape of Christ's care. 'I will keep My eyes on them for good' is the language of a shepherd who does not lose track of the exiled. Jesus' words to His own, that no one will snatch them out of His hand, John 10:28, are the long fulfilment of that attention.

Care is needed. The two baskets are not an allegory of two kinds of Christians and the passage does not say that the bad figs in Jerusalem had no way back, any more than it says the exiles had earned their place. The link to Christ is by promise and pattern: the new heart He gives, the shape of His own path, and the way He sorts the people by the grace they receive.
study.god:
The vision shows a God who sees differently from people. Jeremiah sees figs and says so, 'Figs!', 24:3. God sees which are which, and the interpretation overturns the judgment of the city. The theology of the passage is that God's regard for people is not read off their circumstances. He does not call the exiles good because they were happier or because they had behaved well but because He has decided to deal with them for good, and He explains what that means.

He is the God who sends. 'Whom I have sent away from this place', 24:5. The exile was not a defeat for God by Babylon. It was the LORD's own act, and the Chaldeans were the instrument. That is a hard doctrine and a comforting one: the pain of the exiles was not random, and it was not outside His hand. Because He sent them, He can bring them back.

He is the God who gives the heart. The new heart of 24:7 is His gift, and the sentence is stated in the first person, 'I will give them a heart'. Human repentance in the passage is real, 'they will return to Me with all their heart', but it is the result of divine giving and not its cause. This is one of the clearest statements in the Old Testament that the turning of the heart is itself grace.

He is a covenant God. 'They will be My people, and I will be their God' is the covenant promise in its shortest form, and it is repeated at the heart of the new covenant, 31:33. Even in the middle of judgment, God keeps the language of belonging. The exiles are still His.

He is also just. The bad figs are not an afterthought. God does not soften the verdict on Zedekiah and those who stayed, and the language of the curses in verses 9 and 10 shows that His justice is not suspended by His mercy to the exiles. The sentence that follows from persistence in sin is sword, famine and plague, and the chapter says it will fall until the people have perished from the land.

God is patient in the way He deals with people over time. The vision is given early, before the final fall of Jerusalem, so that Zedekiah and his people have the chance to hear and change. The sorting is a warning as well as a verdict.

For worship, the vision invites trust in a God whose purposes are larger than what our eyes can see. We praise Him not only when things look like blessing but when they look like loss, because He is the one who keeps His eyes on His own for good and who gives, by His own hand, the heart that knows Him.

crossReferences.note: The call of the prophet, 'to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant'. In 24:6 only the building and planting verbs are aimed at the good figs, so the vision applies the commission with each half falling on a different group.

The letter to the exiles puts the vision into practice. The good figs are to build houses, plant gardens and seek the welfare of the city where they are. They are to live as a people who expect a return, but who do not spend their exile waiting only for it.

The same verdict stated again, now to the exiles: the king and the people left in the city will be made like rotten figs, so bad they cannot be eaten. It confirms that chapter 24 was not a private vision but a message meant to be relayed.

The people of Jerusalem call the exiles far from the LORD and claim the land for themselves. God replies that He has been a sanctuary for the exiles and will give them a new heart. It is a close parallel to the figs, from Ezekiel, who was himself in Babylon.

Moses says that to that day the LORD had not given Israel a mind to understand, eyes to see, or ears to hear. Jeremiah 24:7 is the answer: the day will come when God gives the heart. The vision looks back to this lament and forward to the new covenant.

Here the exiles' promise is spelled out in full. The law written within, knowledge of the LORD from the least to the greatest, and forgiveness that remembers sins no more together unfold what it means to be given a heart to know Him.

A new heart, a new spirit and the removal of a heart of stone. Ezekiel adds that God will put His Spirit within, which answers the question of how the heart promised in Jeremiah 24:7 will be made able to obey.

The writer quotes Jeremiah 31 at length and says it is fulfilled in Christ's priestly work. It is the New Testament's confirmation that the heart promised to the exiles is the gift of the new covenant.

God chose the foolish, the weak and the lowly to shame the wise and the strong, so that no one may boast. The good figs are the exiles who were despised in Jerusalem, and Paul describes the same principle at work in the church.

Peter addresses believers as the elect who are exiles. The exile of Jeremiah 24 becomes a picture of the church's condition in the world, chosen and scattered, and cared for by God while it is away from home.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible begins with a man and woman living in the presence of God and ends with a people living in it again. In between lies the long story of exile: Adam driven east of the garden, Israel sent to Babylon, and the church living as a pilgrim people. The vision of the two baskets belongs to that middle part, and it says something the story needs to say: exile is not the place where God is absent.

The vision answers the question that Genesis 3 leaves open, what becomes of those sent away from God's presence. The answer is not that they are abandoned but that God goes with them, plants them and promises to bring them back. In Ezekiel the same promise is that He will be a sanctuary to them in the lands where they have gone, Ezekiel 11:16. The mercy of the first promise, that the seed of the woman will crush the serpent, Genesis 3:15, is already at work here.

What the vision sets up is the new covenant. The gift of a heart to know God is the missing piece of the old arrangement, where the law was given and the heart was not. Jeremiah 31 develops the idea, Ezekiel adds the Spirit, and Christ delivers the promise. Everything in Judah's long history of covenant-breaking is pointing to the need for a heart that does not have to be told to know the LORD.

The story's centre is Christ, who goes into exile in the deepest sense. He is cast out of the city and bears the disgrace outside the camp, Hebrews 13:12-13, so that those who are scattered may be brought near. In Him the verdict on the exiles, that God regards them as good, is made good, for believers are clothed in a righteousness that is not their own.

And the story ends where exile ends. The nations of the new creation are gathered, and God dwells with His people, who will be His people, with God Himself among them as their God, Revelation 21:3. The baskets of figs, with their sorting of one people into two, are finally replaced by a city where nothing unclean enters and the tree of life bears fruit for the healing of the nations, Revelation 22:2. The people who looked like they had lost everything are the ones who inherit it.

quiz.q: Who do the good figs represent in this vision?

options.text: The exiles already carried off to Babylon in the first deportation.
options.note: Verse 5 explicitly identifies the good figs as 'the exiles from Judah' sent to the land of the Chaldeans.

options.text: King Zedekiah and the officials who remained in Jerusalem.
options.note: This group is explicitly identified with the bad figs in verse 8.

options.text: The nations surrounding Judah.
options.note: The vision concerns two groups within Judah itself, not surrounding nations.

options.text: The priests specifically, as distinct from other exiles.
options.note: The good figs represent the exiles generally, not one professional group in particular.

quiz.q: What is surprising or reversing expectations about this vision?

options.text: Those who suffered the apparent loss of exile are marked for God's favor, while those who seemed to remain safely are marked for disaster.
options.note: This overturns the natural assumption that visible hardship signals God's disfavor and safety signals His approval.

options.text: Both baskets of figs turn out to represent the exact same group of people.
options.note: The vision explicitly distinguishes two separate groups with opposite fates.

options.text: The vision shows that all figs, good and bad, are eventually eaten.
options.note: The bad figs are explicitly described as inedible, and the two groups meet very different fates, not the same outcome.

options.text: It shows that Babylon itself will be shown mercy alongside Judah.
options.note: The vision concerns two groups within Judah, not Babylon's own fate.

quiz.q: What specific promise does God make to the good figs in verse 7?

options.text: He will give them a heart to know Him, and they will return to Him with all their heart.
options.note: This is an inward, relational transformation, not merely a change of external circumstance.

options.text: He will give them great material wealth immediately.
options.note: The stated promise centers on a transformed heart and restored relationship, not material wealth.

options.text: He will exempt them from all future hardship of any kind.
options.note: The promise concerns their ultimate restoration and heart transformation, not exemption from all difficulty.

options.text: He will make them rulers over the nations that exiled them.
options.note: The promise is about their return, their heart, and their relationship with God, not political rule over Babylon.

quiz.q: What does God pronounce over Zedekiah and the remnant left in the land?

options.text: He will make them a horror and disgrace among the nations and send sword, famine, and plague against them.
options.note: Verses 8 to 10 pronounce severe judgment on this group, in stark contrast to the promise given the exiles.

options.text: He promises them the same heart transformation given to the exiles.
options.note: This promise is given specifically to the good figs, the exiles, not to Zedekiah's remnant.

options.text: He offers them an immediate opportunity to repent and avoid all judgment.
options.note: The passage pronounces the verdict directly rather than extending a fresh offer within this vision.

options.text: He shows them no different treatment than the exiles at all.
options.note: The two groups are explicitly given opposite fates in this vision.

quiz.q: How does the promise in verse 7 anticipate later revelation?

options.text: It anticipates the fuller new covenant promise in Jeremiah 31, where God writes His law on the heart, ultimately fulfilled through Christ.
options.note: The language of a new heart to know God directly foreshadows Jeremiah 31:33-34 and its New Testament fulfillment.

options.text: It has no connection to any later promise in Scripture.
options.note: The heart-and-knowing language directly parallels and anticipates Jeremiah 31:33-34.

options.text: It anticipates only a return to strict ceremonial law-keeping.
options.note: The promise concerns inward transformation and relationship, not merely external ceremonial observance.

options.text: It anticipates judgment on the exiles rather than restoration.
options.note: The promise here is explicitly restorative and relational, not a further judgment on the exiles.

questions: The exiles who looked like the losers were actually the ones God was preparing for restoration. Where might you be misreading a hard season of your own life as God's disfavor rather than His preparation?
God promised the exiles a new heart to truly know Him, not just a return to their old circumstances. Are you seeking a change in circumstances more than a change of heart?
Zedekiah's remnant presumed on their apparent safety instead of turning to God. Where might you be resting in comfortable circumstances rather than genuine relationship with Him?
This vision shows God's favor does not follow visible appearances. Where do you need to trust God's assessment of your situation over your own?
The promise of a new heart here grows into the full new covenant later in Jeremiah. How have you experienced God giving you a new heart to know Him through Christ?

translationNotes.note: The deportation referenced is the first major exile under Nebuchadnezzar in 597 BC, distinct from the final fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC; this vision is set specifically in that earlier window.
'I regard as good' is a legal or evaluative declaration, not merely an observation; God is formally pronouncing His verdict and intention toward the exiles, not just describing their character.
'A heart to know Me' uses yada, a Hebrew verb for intimate, covenantal knowledge rather than mere intellectual awareness, the same relational sense used of a husband and wife 'knowing' each other.
